opening: How strong is our faith when the security we've depended upon begins to disappear? What happens when we pray, believe in God's love, and yet find ourselves overwhelmed by fear? Perhaps these are the moments when we discover what faith really asks of us.
body:
A few days ago, I found myself in a place I never wanted to be. The reality of losing my career, not having a stable income, and facing an uncertain financial future became overwhelming. I was so consumed by worry that I didn't want to eat or even take care of myself. I simply wanted the day to end.

I love God. I believe in Him. I believe He loves me. Yet that day, I couldn't bring myself to believe He would take care of me.

I didn't feel abandoned. I felt unworthy.

I prayed, but I didn't feel relief. I didn't hear an answer. It was just me, my worries, and a darkness that seemed to take every bit of strength I had.

Then my disability check arrived, a payment I had been anxiously waiting for. And I felt better.

But that left me with a troubling question. Was my peace restored because I trusted God, or simply because the money arrived?

I think it was the money. And admitting that made me question the depth of my faith.

I had always thought I possessed a great deal of faith. But when I needed it most, why couldn't I find it?

Today, reading Ephesians, I encountered something that spoke directly to that struggle.

Paul tells us:

"Put on the armor of God so that you may be able to stand firm against the tactics of the devil."

I could almost physically see myself putting on that armor. Fastening truth around my waist, covering myself with righteousness, preparing my feet with the Gospel of peace, lifting the shield of faith, placing salvation upon my head, and taking up the Word of God.

And for the first time in days, I could imagine facing what lies ahead without being consumed by it.

Paul doesn't promise that life's difficulties will disappear. He tells us to stand firm. He speaks of the flaming arrows that threaten us and the shield of faith that can extinguish them.

I don't believe my financial struggles or the loss of my career are the work of evil. But I do recognize how easily fear can take hold, how despair can overwhelm my thoughts, and how quickly I can lose sight of God's love when uncertainty consumes me.

That is what I need protection against.

For years, I worked in cardiothoracic surgery, caring for patients during some of the most frightening and vulnerable moments of their lives. I tried to give them strength, compassion, and reassurance. I couldn't promise them a successful outcome, but I could offer my knowledge, my presence, and everything I had to give.

I loved that work, even though it was demanding and relentless.

That chapter of my life has ended. I cannot return to the career I once knew, and I have come to accept that. But accepting the loss of my profession doesn't make the financial uncertainty any less frightening.

Now I am the vulnerable one. I am the one who needs reassurance, support, and the courage to face an uncertain future.

And I am learning.

I've learned to ask for what I need, to challenge decisions that seem unjust, and to persist even when the chances of success are slim. I've appealed medical insurance decisions, pursued arbitration over attorney fees, and advocated for accurate disability documentation. I've also begun speaking openly with family and friends about our financial difficulties.

None of these efforts guarantees a favorable outcome. But I continue because I know I must.

Perhaps I have already been learning to stand firm, even on the days when I feel my faith is failing.

Then I read today's Gospel.

The Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill Him. Jesus knows the danger before Him, yet He refuses to turn away from Jerusalem.

He tells them He will continue His work and accomplish His purpose.

Jesus walks forward knowing that suffering and rejection await Him. He doesn't allow fear to determine His direction. He remains faithful to His Father's will.

And suddenly the two readings came together.

Paul tells us how to stand firm. Jesus shows us what that steadfastness looks like.

Jesus doesn't turn away from Jerusalem, and I cannot turn away from the uncertainty before me. I must continue forward, even without knowing how things will turn out.

But I don't have to carry the weight of that uncertainty alone.

My husband often tells me to give my worries to God. It sounds so simple. Yet when the bills remain, the income is uncertain, and prayers seem unanswered, surrender can feel almost impossible.

I am beginning to understand that giving my worries to God doesn't mean I stop being afraid. It means I don't allow that fear to consume me or convince me that I am beyond His care.

And here is the irony.

We imagine armor as something heavy, something we must carry into battle. Yet God's armor feels different. It doesn't add to the weight of my struggles. It gives me the strength to carry what I could never carry alone.

I am reminded of Jesus' words in Luke 11:11:

"What father among you would hand his son a snake when he asks for a fish?"

If we, as imperfect parents, want what is good for our children, how much more does our heavenly Father want what is good for us?

I know this. I believe this. Yet when fear overwhelmed me, I struggled to trust that it applied to me.

Perhaps that is why I need God's armor. Not because He has stopped loving me, but because fear can make me forget just how deeply I am loved.

His armor doesn't make my problems disappear. It protects my heart from losing sight of the Father who loves me.
I don't know what tomorrow will bring. I don't know whether my appeals will succeed, whether my financial security will return, or what this next chapter of my life will look like.

And I know there will be days when fear returns, perhaps with the same intensity.

But I have something to reach for now.

God never promised that I would escape life's battles. He offers me the strength to face them without surrendering my heart to despair.

I can put on His armor, lift my shield of faith, and take the next step.

Not because I know how this story ends, but because I know I am loved by the One who walks with me.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  You know the burdens I carry, the fears I struggle to release, and the moments when my faith feels too weak to sustain me.  Clothe me in Your armor. Fasten truth around me when fear distorts my thoughts. Protect my heart with righteousness, steady my steps with Your peace, and strengthen my shield of faith when despair threatens to overwhelm me.  Teach me to trust Your love even when I cannot see Your hand at work. Give me the courage to persevere without demanding to know the outcome.  And when the weight of life becomes too heavy, remind me that I was never meant to carry it alone.  Amen.
scripture: Ephesians 6:10–20 — The armor of God  Luke 13:31–35 — Jesus continues toward Jerusalem  —  Luke 11:11–13 — The goodness of our heavenly Father
theme: What happens when our faith is tested, our security disappears, and fear begins to overwhelm us? Perhaps God's protection isn't always about removing the battle, but giving us the strength to stand through it.
title: The Irony of God's Armor: It is Light
